rv.q: The end result is certainly the funniest show on Broadway in years, if not the most likable.
He’s the cream in the borscht, the schmaltz in the gribenes, and his prodigious charm makes Mr. Saturday Night a very haimish experience.
And if you’re in search of hilarity, retro good times and Crystal’s now-precious signature smoothie of affirmation, timing and stark comedic honesty, “Mr. Saturday Night” is your show.
So why did I enjoy it so much? When the show isn't trying to be a musical, it puts Crystal up in front of us and has him do Buddy's act.
Crystal understands this brand of self-mocking shtick so well that you instantly feel in the safest of hands.
Crystal's performance is the show's main draw, and he delivers with the easy authority of a seasoned entertainer who knows how to work a room.
The glorious punchlines that have eluded most new musicals are here knocked outta the park by a master.
Sometimes entertainment is a mercifully simple affair.
The chemistry between the brothers – or, more accurately, between real-life pals and long-ago co-stars Crystal and Paymer – is easily the most enjoyable thing in a generally enjoyable production.
As a piece of theater, the show is a bit of a mess; the jokes, even some of the hoary ones, work better than the storytelling, and the acting styles are all over the place.
But there is precious little pulse throughout “Mr. Saturday Night,” a double shot at redemption for both Buddy and his marquee creator.
But unless you are on-board with a throwback to 1990s Crystal comedy, it delivers more groans than laughs.

What is surprising, given that no one really asked for this, and considering the general soullessness of such reboots, is how perfectly charming and entertaining the work is.

Crystal delivers the kind of star performance that has been mostly missing from Broadway this season and which audiences are eating up with a giant teaspoon.
If you love Billy Crystal, book a ticket. He's funny, charming, not grandstanding.
But for those looking for a Broadway show that's livelier than a Catskills performance, you might have a hard time finding it.
Do you enjoy watching Billy Crystal do what he does better than anybody, weaponizing punchlines and detonating them for explosive laughs?

But they exist uneasily together, and wind up undermining one another, not least because the running time of about 170 minutes (including intermission) — way longer than the movie — is too long for a light, sentimental comedy that gets its juice from quick-hit Borscht Belt humor.
However, anyone else may find this decent show to be a tired affair which just about sustains its two-and-half-hour running time.
He’s so assured—in the perhaps forgotten manner of George Burns and George Jessel—he compensates sufficiently to make himself Mr. Every Night of the Week.
But there’s nothing about the musical that displays a reason for being, other than to showcase its star’s extraordinary comic chops.

But along with the rest of the creative team, including director John Rando (Urinetown), who guides the less-than-deluxe-looking production, the songwriters haven't presented a compelling argument that Buddy's story expands as a musical.

While Crystal and the cast are droll and endearing, “Mr. Saturday Night” (directed by John Rando with an especially small cast for an old-fashioned-style musical comedy) is pretty dull, slow, and schmaltzy.
At its heart, the musical “Mr. Saturday Night” is as sentimental as it is dishonest.
Now the book is silly, often crude, a bit vulgar, a bit TV, with jokes as dated as the Borscht belt routines he started out with.
Unfortunately the show has limited audience appeal and I can’t see a younger audience enjoying this the way their parents and grandparents would.

So while there are the occasional bursts of brilliance, as in Graff singing “Tahiti” while in a daydream, unfortunately, as a whole there isn’t quite the musical comedy magic we’d expect from a collaboration between veteran composers like Brown and stars like Crystal, Paymer, and Graff.
The sometimes schmaltzy book and characters are undeniably old-fashioned, geared to traditional old-time Broadway audiences.

cn.t: Crystal charms with expert comic timing in this nostalgic but uneven musical adaptation, delivering Borscht Belt laughs that delight its target audience even as critics find the show overstuffed, dated, and dramatically thin.

sg.ra: The Nederlander is a relatively compact 1,232-seat 1921 Walter C. Jordan house (architect William Neil Smith) with a shallow orchestra rake, so you want to sit forward of where the problems begin; center rows B-E sit forward of the mezz overhang (which becomes notable at row M) and forward of where the shallow rake starts costing shorter patrons their sightlines, giving a direct center look at the 86-ft-wide stage.

sg.vl: Smart value under the overhang line
sg.ra: The Nederlander mezz overhang is 'notable by row M and cuts into the stage at row Q,' so center rows L-O sit just on the safe side of that line - you get a sub-premium price in a 1921 house known historically for being overlooked on its lone 41st Street block (the southernmost Broadway theater), without the shallow-rake head-blocking that plagues the back half.

sg.vl: Where the overhang eats the stage
sg.ra: This is the Nederlander-specific trap: the mezz overhang 'cuts into the stage at row Q,' and the 1921 orchestra's shallow rake means a tall patron in front of you is a real problem - one Redwood patron reported the overhang 'cuts off about the top 20% of the stage,' which mattered because that show featured climbing a redwood; skip for anything with vertical staging or flying effects.

The Nederlander's mezz is raked steeply enough that sightlines stay clean even though you're in a 1921 house without an elevator - rows BB and CC beat row AA because AA has a safety bar across the front that 'may be too high for shorter theatergoers' and 'can cut into the stage'; the center front mezz here looks down into the 40-ft proscenium cleanly.

Multiple guides single out the last two front-mezz rows (DD, EE) as the best 'value for money' at the Nederlander - you're still in the front mezz bloc with the steep mezz rake that keeps the 1921 house's sightlines clean, but priced below rows AA-CC; the tradeoff is legroom which is tight across the mezz here.

The Nederlander has no balcony - the rear mezz is the top tier - and the house is a compact 1,232 seats, so even the 'farthest' seat isn't far; the mezz rake stays steep enough that middle seats FF-JJ hold up, and this is the southernmost Broadway theater (208 W 41st, unusually isolated from the 44th-45th Street cluster), which typically keeps these prices lower than comparable rear-mezz at flagship houses.

sg.vl: Last rows of a no-elevator house
sg.ra: The Nederlander has 'no elevators or escalators' - a 1921 house quirk that matters when you're climbing to rows KK-PP - and a Tripadvisor thread flagged that row JJ sits above a stairwell entryway with a railing bar that can intrude; beyond JJ you're in the last stretch of a 10-row rear mezz (FF-PP) with tight legroom and the most angled sightlines in the house, and this is the top tier since there's no balcony.
